Project 2: Built-in symmetry
Take a network built for a symmetry of its data, build it, and show what the symmetry buys
1
Form a group and choose a network within a week: at most 3 people, and at most two 5000-level students in a group. For example, two 5000-level students and one 4000-level student is fine.
2
Build it in PyTorch (libraries are fine) and draw it in Torch Canvas style.
3
Train it and a baseline on the HPC. Show learning curves, data efficiency and a symmetry test.
4
Publish a pip-installable repo with both models’ weights and a small test sample.
5
Present: 18 minutes, strictly, then 7 minutes of round-robin questions. Everyone presents and everyone answers.
GRADING
Only the presentation is graded, but the models must load and run. We install your repo with pip and run one short script; untested code that doesn't run gets no points.
5000-level: a group with a 5000-level student picks from Going beyond.
4000-level: working on a Going beyond network earns +15 extra credit on the project.
Spend your minutes on what's new; give what we already know one sentence.

Project 3: A specialist vs. a generalist
Design a model for your own problem, then pit it against an adapted foundation model
1 · PROPOSE, WITHIN 12 DAYS
One paragraph: the problem and its data source. Email it to Jtroberts@tntech.edu, cc ntherron42@tntech.edu; we reply with feedback.
An ongoing project can be acceptable.
2 · BUILD THE SPECIALIST
Design it for the data, task and invariances, informed by the literature. Train it on the HPC with intentional augmentation, regularization, learning-rate schedule and early stopping.
3 · COMPARE, LAST
Adapt the most appropriate foundation model for your domain with full fine-tuning or PEFT, and compare fairly.
We cover foundation models and adaptation on Nov 17, so this comes last.
  • Why now? Finding a problem and data takes time, and HPC runs take longer. Starting today gives you six weeks.
  • You don't know foundation models yet, and that's fine. Nothing before step 3 needs them, and we'll cover them before you get there.
You don't have to win. How you design and train is what's graded.

Padding shrinks the variance at the edges
σ²ŷ at each of the 14 × 14 positions, with the ring of padding zeros around it. Slide the same 3 × 3 filter to two places.
σ²ŷ 0.4
2.1white = 1
IN THE MIDDLE
All 9 filter weights land on real inputs, in each of the 32 channels.
σ²ŷ = Cin · k² · σW² · E[p̂²]
    = 32 · 9 · (2/288) · ½ = 1
measured 1.00
ON THE CORNER
5 of the 9 filter weights land on padding zeros, and a zero adds nothing to the sum. Only (k − 1)² = k² − 2k + 1 = 4 real terms remain.
σ²ŷ = Cin · (k² − 2k + 1) · σW² · E[p̂²]
    = 32 · 4 · (2/288) · ½ = 4/9 ≈ 0.44
measured 0.44
Along an edge, 3 weights land on zeros: k² − k = 6 real terms, σ²ŷ = 6/9 ≈ 0.67 (measured 0.66).
You could correct it: scale each output by (k²/N)1/2, with N the real inputs under the filter. At a corner, ×1.5.
Fewer real terms in the sum, less variance. PyTorch doesn't correct for it.

A conv is a local linear layer with tied weights
Unroll a 1-D, one-channel, conv with a 3-weight filter on 8 positions into the matrix it really is.
Forward: ŷ = p̂ Wᵀ
Local: zeros off the band.

Tied: one color per diagonal, the same 3 weights in every column.

Each column of Wᵀ, dotted with all of p̂, fills one entry of ŷ. The zeros wipe out 5 products, leaving 3: the fan-in.
Backward: ∂L/∂p̂ = ∂L/∂ŷ W
Same shapes: each gradient has the shape of its variable.

A column of W is a row of Wᵀ: the 3 outputs that p̂ fed, the fan-out.

Read down it: w₃ w₂ w₁, a conv with the filter flipped.
Same multiply and sum as a linear layer, so the same variance rules. Backprop just multiplies by W instead of Wᵀ.

Variance through a pool: forward
2 × 2 windows, stride 2. The input has mean 0 and σ² = 1.
Average: a sum of 4 terms with every weight ¼, so the conv rule applies: σ² = 4 · (¼)² · 1 = ¼.
Max: the winner had to beat three others, so it sits higher and spreads less. The largest of 4 standard normals has mean 1.03 and σ² 0.49, computed from its distribution, 4φ(x)Φ(x)³, and matched by measurement.
Both pools shrink the variance, and max also shifts the mean. The GroupNorm after each pool resets both.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Where the max pool's 0.49 comes from
The max of a 2 × 2 window is the largest of 4 independent standard normals.
1
One value. Each of the 4 values in the window is N(0, 1). The chance one is at most x is Φ(x), the area under the bell curve to the left of x.
2
The max is at most x exactly when all four are at most x. The four are independent, so multiply:
P(max ≤ x) = Φ(x) · Φ(x) · Φ(x) · Φ(x) = Φ(x)⁴
3
Its density is the derivative: f(x) = 4 Φ(x)³ φ(x). Read it as: one of the 4 values lands at x (4 choices, density φ), and the other 3 fall below it (Φ³).
4
Mean and variance are the usual integrals, done numerically:
μ = ∫ x f(x) dx = 1.03    σ² = ∫ (x − μ)² f(x) dx = 0.49
At x = 1, one value is below it 84% of the time, but all four only 50% of the time: the max of 4 sits around 1.
A bigger window, n values: P(max ≤ x) = Φ(x)n, so the max moves further right and spreads even less.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Variance through a pool: backward
The gradient g arrives at one output. Where does it go in the window?
Max: only the winner gets g; the other three get 0. Over the four inputs, E[(∂L/∂x)²] = ¼ · E[g²].
Average: all four get g/4. E[(∂L/∂x)²] = (¼)² · E[g²].
The residual skips route around the convs, not around the pools, so these cuts compound: two max pools, ÷16.
Max pooling sends gradient to only the winner. Remember that.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Variance through the whole network: forward
Tuesday's CNN at init (stem σW² = 1/25, He for the block convs). Blue: ideal σ² (E[p̂²] after a ReLU) and distribution.
Every branch starts with a GroupNorm: N(0, 1). ReLU keeps half, E[p̂²] = ½, with a spike at 0; each He-init conv brings σ² back to 1.
Each branch adds 1 to the stream. A max pool of independent values shifts the distribution right and keeps σ² × 0.49: .49 → 1.47, pool → .74 → 1.71 → 2.68.
The head's GroupNorm resets to N(0, 1); the average pool then narrows it to a tight bump.
The stream grows by about 1 per block, but every branch and the head see σ² = 1, because each starts with a norm.
Variance through the whole network: forward
Tuesday's CNN at init (stem σW² = 1/25, He for the block convs). Blue: ideal σ² (E[p̂²] after a ReLU) and distribution. Orange: measured on 512 digits.
Max pools barely shrink the real stream (.89 → .90, 1.88 → 2.02): neighboring pixels are nearly equal, so the max of 4 is close to any one of them.
Each branch still adds about 1: .90 → 1.88, 2.02 → 3.16 → 4.41. The real stream is right-skewed, not normal.
The first ReLU in each block keeps about 0.64, not ½: its GroupNorm normalizes that skewed stream. A norm fixes the mean and variance, not the shape.
The stream grows by about 1 per block, but every branch and the head see σ² = 1, because each starts with a norm.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Variance through the whole network: backward
Same network, gradients flowing back. Numbers: E[(∂L/∂·)²] per element, with ∂L/∂out of variance 1; µ = ×10⁻⁶. Blue: ideal.
Head: Linear ×10/32 → 0.31; the avg pool spreads it over 49 positions, ÷49²; ReLU ×½ (a spike of zeros); GroupNorm ÷σ²(X₃) = ÷2.68.
Each + passes the gradient straight back, and its branch adds its own share, which GroupNorm scales by 1/σ² of the stream: big where the pools shrank the stream. 24.3µ → 38.5µ → 90.3µ.
Each max pool: ÷4, with 3 of every 4 gradients exactly 0 (90.3µ → 22.6µ). The stem conv ×32 back to the image.
Gradients flow back along the stream almost unchanged. The pools shrink them; the norms set each branch's share.
Variance through the whole network: backward
Same network, gradients flowing back. Numbers: E[(∂L/∂·)²] per element, with ∂L/∂out of variance 1; µ = ×10⁻⁶. Blue: ideal. Orange: measured.
The real stream has a bigger σ² (the pools barely shrank it), so GroupNorm divides by more and the branches add less: 13.3µ → 16.7µ → 22.2µ, not 90.3µ.
The pool still zeroes 3 in 4 (75% exactly 0 measured) and cuts E² by 4: 22.2µ → 5.5µ.
Shapes: after a ReLU or a pool, most of the gradient is a spike at 0; elsewhere it is close to normal.
Gradients flow back along the stream almost unchanged. The pools shrink them; the norms set each branch's share.
Variance through the whole network: backward
Same network, gradients flowing back. Numbers: E[(∂L/∂·)²] per element, with ∂L/∂out of variance 1; µ = ×10⁻⁶. Blue: ideal. Orange: measured.
At the weights, the sum brings it back. ∂L/∂W = Σ g · p̂ over every position of every image: 512 × 14 × 14 = 100,352 products per weight in block 1, 25,088 in blocks 2 and 3.
Per-entry g (rms) → weight gradient (rms): block 1: 0.0022 → 1.21, 0.0024 → 1.37; block 2: 0.0038 → 1.18, 0.0041 → 1.26; block 3: 0.0032 → 1.05, 0.0036 → 1.30.
‖∂L/∂W‖ / ‖W‖ ≈ 10–16 in every conv, stem to block 3: no layer is starved. (Large overall because this loss sums over the 512 images.)
Gradients flow back along the stream almost unchanged. The pools shrink them; the norms set each branch's share.

SAME STORY AS RELU → SILU
A hard gate passes gradient only where it is open. Smooth the gate, and every input learns, even the ones it mostly shuts.
A soft gate: every value hears how it should change.

When is the biggest value the wrong one?
Talk it over with a neighbour before we move on
?
Soft or hard, the pool still scores each value by its own size. When would you want the gate to favour something other than the loudest value?
When loud isn't relevant
A thick, bright stroke fires hard, but a 7 and a 1 both have one. The faint top bar is what tells them apart. Relevance belongs to the task, not to the size of the value.
When relevance depends on context
Whether an edge matters depends on what else is in the image: a short bar at the top means one thing above a diagonal and another above a loop.
Split the job in two: one learned projection scores, another supplies the value. The second card needs more: that's Nov 10.
"Biggest" was only ever a stand-in. Let the network learn the score.

© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Fixed mixing vs. input-dependent mixing
Both are learned. The question is whether the mixing weights change from image to image.
Convolution
out = V · w
wj is set by where pixel j sits in the window: top-left always gets the same weight.
Learned once in training, then the same for every image and every window.
Linear in V.
Gated pooling (SoftPool, attention pooling)
out = V · g(V)
g(V) is set by what the pixels contain: computed fresh for each window of each image.
The learned part is the rule for making weights (w), not the weights themselves.
Not linear in V: the input multiplies itself through the gate.
Gated pooling is still local and still uses the same w and V in every window. On Nov 10 we let a window's gate depend on the other windows too.
A conv mixes by position; a gate mixes by content.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
Does it matter on MNIST?
Tuesday's network with both pools swapped. Full MNIST, 6 epochs, 3 seeds each.
Circles: one seed each. Bar: the mean. Gradient share measured at initialization.
LET EACH CHANNEL LEARN τ
Started at τ = 1, ended between 0.89 and 1.12. Adam could have moved it 10× either way. The push kept flipping: the network has no preference.
All six land within 0.3 points, about the spread between seeds. Max learns as well as the soft gates while only a quarter of its inputs ever hear a gradient.
Every input learns, but MNIST doesn't need a smarter gate. A learned score needs a harder question.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
What to take away
Max pooling is a gate, in three lines
01
Convs keep variance with fan-in and fan-out of k² × channels. Pools change it, and max sends gradient to only the winner.
02
Max pooling is hardmax times the values. Soften it: SoftPool. Give it gate and value projections: attention pooling.
03
A stride-2 conv mixes with fixed weights; a gate mixes with weights the input chooses.
Pooling is a gate over positions, and gates can be learned.

A learned score, but for whom?
One w gives the whole image one ranking. Different positions need different things.
One learned w
sj = xj wᵀ
The score of position j doesn't depend on who is pooling. If the bar scores highest, it wins for everyone: the corner, the stem, the background.

Split the score in two
sij = qi · kj
Query qi: what position i, the one pooling, is looking for.
Key kj: what position j, the one being considered, has to offer.
Context comes in through the query: the same bar can matter to the corner and not to the background.
GLU's gate read one token. This gate reads two: the one asking and the one being asked about.
Split the gate's weights into a query half and a key half.

CNN: global only through depth
receptive field = 1 + L(k − 1)
With 5 × 5 filters at stride 1, a unit needs 7 layers to see all 28 pixels. Pooling speeds that up, but parts of the digit far apart only meet late.

j = 1 … t, every position
Every token can pool from every other token in a single step. The bottom of the stem can look straight at the top bar.

One token per pixel of a 224 × 224 photo: 2.5 × 10⁹ gates, about 10 GB at 4 bytes each, for one image, one head, one layer. Grouping pixels into 16 × 16 patches cuts that by a factor of about 65,000.
Global costs t². That is why a ViT starts by cutting the image into patches.

Attention is equivariant to every reordering of the tokens, not just shifts
P̂ reorders the same way
attn(shuffle(X)) = shuffle(attn(X))
Measured on the trained layer with the 7's tokens: largest difference 1.1 × 10⁻⁵, which is float rounding.
After the global average pool the order is gone entirely: the prediction is identical (invariant).
WHY
Look at sij = qi · kj. Nothing in it says where token j sits, only what it contains. The weights are shared by every token, so a token's place in the list never enters the computation.

Like the CNN, no weight has an address. Unlike the CNN, nothing knows who its neighbours are.
To this layer, the 7 and its scrambled tokens are the same input. Our stem is still local, so the inside of each token keeps its order; a ViT has nothing like that beyond the patch. Part 2 gives back the "where": positional embeddings.
Attention scores what a token is, never where it is.

Less built in, more data needed
Tuesday's trade-off, one more rung: what each layer assumes about images
MLP
Every weight has an address. Assumes nothing about neighbours or shifts.
Pixel shuffle: doesn't care.
CNN
Same filter everywhere, and locality: neighbours belong together. Shift-equivariant.
Pixel shuffle: breaks it.
Attention
Same weights for every token, but no locality and no position. Equivariant to every reordering.
Token shuffle: can't even tell.
VISION TRANSFORMER vs. RESNET, IMAGENET TOP-1 · DOSOVITSKIY ET AL. (ICLR 2021)
Pretrain on ImageNet (1.3 M images): the ResNets win.
ImageNet-21k (14 M): about even.
JFT-300M (300 M): ViT-H/14 88.55% vs. ResNet (BiT-L) 87.54%.
"Transformers lack some of the inductive biases inherent to CNNs, such as translation equivariance and locality."
Attention trades locality for reach. The data has to supply what the layer doesn't assume.

WHERE THE ANALOGY STRETCHES
Max pooling had no query. The value scored itself. The query is the new idea, not a detail.
One gate per pair, not per channel. GLU gated each channel; attention gives each pair one number (one per head, in part 2).
No shrinking. Strided pooling makes the map smaller; attention gives back t tokens for t tokens.
Prior work on this view: Stand-Alone Self-Attention (Ramachandran et al., 2019); Gated Attention Unit (Hua et al., 2022).
Same computation, two vocabularies. Know both.

What to take away
From max pooling to attention, in three lines
01
Pooling is a gate over positions. Attention makes it soft, learned, and set by who is asking.
02
GLU's gate weights split into a query and a key. √d is the temperature that keeps the gate soft.
03
Attention is global in one layer and blind to position: it costs t² and needs data for what it doesn't assume.
Attention: a soft, learned pool that every token runs for itself.
